explanations.explanation: That's right, friend. Ezekiel, a priest (Ezekiel 1:3), says, "the Spirit entered me and set me on my feet." He had just fallen facedown before the glory of the LORD (Ezekiel 1:28), so a boost was welcome. I think he could use all the help standing he could get.

It's actually True, friend. Ezekiel, a priest (Ezekiel 1:3), says, "the Spirit entered me and set me on my feet." He had just fallen facedown before the glory of the LORD (Ezekiel 1:28). Then the Spirit stood him back up, no gym membership needed.

explanations.answer: Them and their fathers to this day
explanations.explanation: Yes, and the LORD says it plainly: "To this very day they and their fathers have rebelled against Me." This isn't a new problem. It's a family habit passed down like a recipe nobody wanted. Ezekiel is walking into a long story.

explanations.answer: Only them since the exile began
explanations.explanation: Close, but the LORD reaches further back than that. He says, "To this very day they and their fathers have rebelled against Me." The fathers are in it too. So the rebelling didn't start when the exile did.

explanations.answer: Only their kings for a few years
explanations.explanation: The LORD doesn't point at a few kings here. He says, "they and their fathers," and He calls the whole thing a rebellious nation. The rebelling has gone on "to this very day," not for just a few years. It's a bigger crowd than one palace.

That's it, baker. The LORD says, "they will know that a prophet has been among them," and He says it whether they listen or refuse to listen. So Ezekiel's job doesn't hang on how the crowd reacts. His job is to show up and speak.
Not a king, friend. The LORD says "a prophet has been among them." Ezekiel isn't sent to rule anybody. He's sent to say, "This is what the Lord GOD says."

Good guess, but the word is prophet. The LORD says, "they will know that a prophet has been among them." Ezekiel isn't there to sit behind a bench and bang a gavel. He's there to speak the LORD's words, listen or not.

It's actually False, friend. The LORD calls them a rebellious house three times in these verses. He tells Ezekiel, "Do not be afraid, though briers and thorns surround you, and you dwell among scorpions." Nobody says that to a man moving into a quiet cul-de-sac.

Right. The LORD never promises easy. He says, "Do not be afraid of their words or dismayed by their presence, though they are a rebellious house." He doesn't take the rough crowd away. He tells Ezekiel not to fear them.

You've got it. The LORD says, "But speak My words to them, whether they listen or refuse to listen, for they are rebellious." Ezekiel's part is to say the words. How people take them isn't his to control.
Hiding is the opposite of what the LORD says here. He tells Ezekiel, "But speak My words to them, whether they listen or refuse to listen." No ducking behind the counter.
No softening in this order, friend. The LORD says, "speak My words to them," His words, as given. Ezekiel isn't asked to turn the heat down so the dough is easier to chew.

explanations.answer: Open his mouth and eat what he's given
explanations.explanation: That's right. The LORD says, "Open your mouth and eat what I give you." It comes right after "Do not be rebellious like that rebellious house." So the answer to rebelling is opening up and taking what the LORD hands over.

explanations.answer: Tear his robe and sit in the dust
explanations.explanation: Nothing about robes or dust here. The LORD's next words are, "Open your mouth and eat what I give you." Ezekiel's next move is a mouth-opening one.

explanations.answer: Go and wash in the River Kebar
explanations.explanation: The River Kebar does come up in this passage, but not here (Ezekiel 3:15). Right after the warning, the LORD says, "Open your mouth and eat what I give you." No washing, just opening wide.

Yes, baker. The words on the front and back are "lamentation, mourning, and woe." That's a lot of ink on both sides, and none of it light reading. Hold onto that, because the taste surprises him next.
That would be a nicer scroll, friend, but it's not this one. The text says the words were "lamentation, mourning, and woe." Front and back, no empty space for the happy stuff.
Not a rulebook this time. The scroll holds "words of lamentation, mourning, and woe." It's written on the front and the back, so there's no flipping it over for a cheerier page.
That's it. Ezekiel says, "So I opened my mouth, and He fed me the scroll." He doesn't argue or stall. He opens up, just as the LORD told him to.
It's actually True, friend. Ezekiel says, "So I opened my mouth, and He fed me the scroll." He does what he's told, with his mouth wide open and the LORD feeding him.

Yes! Ezekiel says, "it was as sweet as honey in my mouth." The words on the scroll were lamentation, mourning and woe, and still it tasted sweet. I can't explain that one, and I'm not going to pretend I can. I'll just say the text says it.
That fits the words on the scroll, friend, but it's not what the text says. Ezekiel says, "it was as sweet as honey in my mouth." The scroll is full of woe and it still tastes sweet.
You'd expect dry from something so heavy, wouldn't you? But Ezekiel says, "it was as sweet as honey in my mouth." The taste doesn't match the words, and that's what makes it stand out.

It's actually False, friend. The LORD says the opposite: "Surely if I had sent you to them, they would have listened to you." The peoples with the hard-to-understand languages would have listened. It's the house of Israel who won't.

That's right. The LORD says, "Surely if I had sent you to them, they would have listened to you." Peoples Ezekiel couldn't even understand would have listened. Meanwhile his own people, who share his language, won't.

explanations.answer: Because they won't listen to the LORD
explanations.explanation: Yes. The LORD says, "the house of Israel will be unwilling to listen to you, since they are unwilling to listen to Me." So it isn't about Ezekiel at all. They're turning away from the One who sent him.

explanations.answer: Because Ezekiel is a stranger to them
explanations.explanation: The text gives a different reason. The LORD says they "are unwilling to listen to Me." Ezekiel is sent to his own people, the exiles (Ezekiel 3:11), so he's no stranger. It's a heart problem, not a name-tag problem.

explanations.answer: Because his message is full of woe
explanations.explanation: That's a fair guess with a scroll like that, friend. But the LORD's reason is this: "since they are unwilling to listen to Me." He ties it to their unwillingness to listen to Him. The woe isn't named as the reason.

Yes. The LORD says, "I will make your face as hard as their faces, and your forehead as hard as their foreheads." Ezekiel gets a match for what he's facing. And since the LORD is the one doing the hardening, Ezekiel isn't going in with only his own strength.

Nothing about his words or voice getting hardened. The LORD says, "I will make your face as hard as their faces, and your forehead as hard as their foreheads." The toughness lands on his face and forehead.
Hands and feet aren't on the list, friend. The LORD says, "I will make your face as hard as their faces, and your forehead as hard as their foreheads." It's all about the face and forehead.

Yep. The LORD says, "I will make your forehead like a diamond, harder than flint." Then He adds, "Do not be afraid of them or dismayed at their presence." That's a forehead you could stamp a thousand cookies with.
It's actually True, friend. The LORD says, "I will make your forehead like a diamond, harder than flint." Then He repeats it again: "Do not be afraid of them or dismayed at their presence."

That's right. The LORD says, "Go to your people, the exiles; speak to them and tell them, 'This is what the Lord GOD says.'" The word is exiles. He's still told to speak, whether they listen or refuse to listen.
Ezekiel is a priest (Ezekiel 1:3), so I see why you went there. But the LORD says, "Go to your people, the exiles." That's who he's sent to.
Not elders this time, friend. The LORD says, "Go to your people, the exiles; speak to them." The word is exiles, and it's the whole group He means.

explanations.answer: Wings and wheels of the living creatures
explanations.explanation: Yes. Ezekiel says it was "the sound of the wings of the living creatures brushing against one another and the sound of the wheels beside them, a great rumbling sound." Those living creatures were part of the vision that dropped him facedown (Ezekiel 1:28). Same glory, same sound system.

explanations.answer: Hooves and chariots on the road
explanations.explanation: I get the thought, since a rumble that big sounds like traffic. But Ezekiel says it was "the sound of the wings of the living creatures brushing against one another and the sound of the wheels beside them." No road, no hooves.

explanations.answer: Voices and harps of the exiles
explanations.explanation: Close on the voices, but not the source. Ezekiel says it was "the sound of the wings of the living creatures brushing against one another and the sound of the wheels beside them, a great rumbling sound." The exiles are down the road at Tel-abib, still waiting for him.

explanations.answer: In bitterness and anger of spirit
explanations.explanation: That's right. Ezekiel says, "I went in bitterness and in the anger of my spirit, with the strong hand of the LORD upon me." The text doesn't say why. I think carrying that scroll of woe to a hard-hearted crowd would stir up plenty.

explanations.answer: In gladness and joy of heart
explanations.explanation: I'd have liked that for him, friend, but it's not what the text says. Ezekiel says, "I went in bitterness and in the anger of my spirit." Still, the strong hand of the LORD is upon him the whole way.

explanations.answer: In peace and quiet of mind
explanations.explanation: Not a peaceful ride, baker. Ezekiel says, "I went in bitterness and in the anger of my spirit, with the strong hand of the LORD upon me." The hand of the LORD is there, even while his spirit is stirred up.

Yes. Ezekiel says that for seven days he "sat where they sat and remained there among them, overwhelmed." He doesn't rush off or start a speech. I think after the scroll and that rumble, he just needed to sit with it.
No party at Tel-abib, friend. Ezekiel says he "sat where they sat and remained there among them, overwhelmed." The word is overwhelmed, and it lasts seven days.
Oh, he was bothered. Ezekiel says he "sat where they sat and remained there among them, overwhelmed." Seven days of sitting, and not one of them unbothered.
